idiom_name: last-expression value, tap, and Hash#[]= returning the stored value
implementation_notes: In Ruby a method's value is the value of its last expression, so returning something is the default and the pattern becomes a question of making that value intentional: end with the object the caller wants, or with an explicit nil when there is nothing interesting to report. The core library supplies both realizations - Object#tap yields self to a block and returns self, so a side step can sit inside a chain, and Hash#[]= returns the value it stored, so an assignment is usable as an expression. Because whatever statement happens to be last becomes the API, methods whose result is meant to be ignored should end in nil (or self for chaining) deliberately.
code_sketch:
def top_component
  container ? container.top_component : self   # ^self: the caller uses it
end

user = User.new("ann").tap { |u| log.info("created #{u.id}") }
price = config[:price] = compute_price          # the value is returned
pitfalls: Whatever is last wins: adding a puts or log line at the end of a method changes its return value to nil (or to the collection, for each) with no error anywhere.
Bang methods signal 'nothing changed' with nil (String#gsub! returns nil when nothing matched), so using a bang method's value as a truth test is a classic bug.
each returns the receiver while map returns a new array, so chaining on the wrong one quietly operates on the unchanged collection.
